newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel mulls plan for Jewish homes in Arab area.
newsitem.headline: Israel mulls plan for Jewish homes in Arab area.

text.p: Israel said on Sunday it was considering a plan for Jewish housing in the heart of an Arab East Jerusalem neighbourhood that Palestinians warned could provoke an explosion of violence.

A government official said the plan for the privately funded project went to the Jerusalem district planning commission on Sunday for the hearing of objections. It will decided whether to send it to the minister for final approval.

An Israeli peace group, Palestinians and a minister in the previous Labour government who had blocked the scheme warned approval by the present rightwing Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could provoke violence.

"Implementation of this decision would mean the destruction of the peace process and the creation of a popular reaction that would make the tunnel incidents a simple matter," the leading PLO official in Jerusalem, Faisal al-Husseini, told Reuters.
"We are trying to deal with this issue in political and peaceful means through the peace process," he said.
Israel's opening of an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem sites in Jerusalem in September -- also rejected by the previous government -- touched off clashes that killed 75 people.
Deputy Housing Minister Meir Porush, asked if the housing plan was wise, said he was not worried.
"I don't see any reason why Jews can't live in the Old City or in the east of the city. There is no reason not to...It can lead to coexistence," he told Israel Radio.
The radio said the plan called for 132 homes for Jews in the Ras al-Amud neighbourhood of Arab East Jerusalem, captured by Israel along with the rest of the West Bank in 1967.
Interior Minister Eliahu Suissa had linked approval of more housing for Arabs in the neighbourhood to approval of the plan for Jewish housing, the radio said.

Lawyer Daniel Siedemann, who opposed the plan at the Sunday hearing on behalf of Israeli peace group Ir Shalem and Palestinians, told Reuters the plan did "not respect the delicate mosaic of the city".
"The linkage between the Jewish and Arab building is scandalous and illegal...they (Arabs) are being held hostage," he added.
Siedeman said the commission could take "a day or a month" before deciding whether to send the plan for Suissa's signature.
Opposition member of parliament Uzi Baram said the plan, which he blocked when he was interior minister in Israel's last government, was a prescription for trouble: "I'm completely against it."

"The hostility that pre-exists in my opinion will also cause a very complicated international problem for the Netanyahu government and it will also cause serious conflicts between the Jews and Arabs in that neighbourhood," he told Israel Radio.

The status of the eastern half the city, which Palestinians want to be the capital of a future Palestinian state, is supposed to be settled in Israeli-Palestinians negotiations that have not resumed since Netanyahu took office in June.
There are now some 160,000 Jews living in East Jerusalem, most in neighbourhoods built for Jews since 1967, amid 155,000 Palestinians.

While all Israeli governments have built housing for Jews in the eastern part of the city since 1967 to reinforce its claim to the area, the previous government did not place Jewish homes in the heart of existing Arab neighbourhoods.
